title: Reinforcement Learning with Multi-Step Lookahead Information Via Adaptive Batching
claim: Naive fixed-batching and MPC heuristics fail on diagnostic environments where exploiting deep lookahead exponentially boosts reward value.
layout: 2 panels, top-down trees, side-by-side, math labels under leaves
description: Two black-and-white tree diagrams side by side, both rooted at a circled start state s_1. The left panel shows s_1 leading to a root s_r, which branches into a binary tree of small filled action nodes. Dashed arrows lead to a row of eight empty leaf circles. A label gives tree depth = ℓ. Below it a caption reads 'A^{ℓ-1} leaves s_leaf, each with A actions, independent Ber(A^{-ℓ}) rewards'. The right panel splits s_1 into two branches. The left branch has reward R_Tr = 0 and leads to a similar tree. The right branch has reward R_L and leads down a single chain to an endpoint s^Y. Labels mark 'tree/line depth = ℓ', 'A^{ℓ-1} leaves s^X' and 'one line endpoint'. The eye goes first to the top circles, then down the branching trees. There is no color.
caption: The diagnostic environments in Claims 2.1 and 2.2. Both environments have deterministic transitions, start at state s1, and are of horizon ℓ+ 1. Rewards are zero except at the last step (and at the first step in Figure 1b as a tie-breaking mechanism). In both cases, observing Bernoulli rewards Ber(A−ℓ) from the root of a full tree exponentially augments their value: to collect a unit reward, only one leaf needs to realize R = 1, which happens w.p. ≥1 −1/e. Observing rewards later in the tree, or not leveraging this exponential increase, is what makes fixed-batching and MPC fail.
abstract: We study tabular finite-horizon reinforcement learning problems with multiple steps of lookahead information. Before acting, the learner observes $\ell$ steps of future transition and reward realizations: the exact state the agent would reach and the rewards it would collect under any possible course of action. While it has been shown that such information can drastically boost the value, finding the optimal policy is NP-hard, and it is common to apply one of two tractable heuristics: processing the lookahead in chunks of predefined sizes ('fixed batching policies'), and model predictive control. We first illustrate the problems with these two approaches and propose utilizing the lookahead in adaptive (state-dependent) batches; we refer to such policies as adaptive batching policies (ABPs). We derive the optimal Bellman equations for these strategies and design an optimistic regret-minimizing algorithm that enables learning the optimal ABP when interacting with unknown environments. Our regret bounds are order-optimal up to a potential factor of the lookahead horizon $\ell$, which can usually be considered a small constant.
